commodities: Eastern goods including furs, wax, grain and timber moved west; western cloth, spices, silk and salt moved east. These are corridor-level categories, not quantified Peterhof totals.
name: Peterhof
notes: Primary witness: Latvian State Historical Archives, Fonds 673, Directory 4, Box 18, no. 7; UNESCO nomination dossier pp. 10–11. place_id remains pending until KAN-306 creates the Novgorod gazetteer row. Commodity categories come from the dossier’s network overview and are explicitly not local totals.
profile_summary:
Peterhof makes the distinction between a Kontor and a colony especially clear. The Second Novgorod Schra, preserved in a Riga copy dated before 1298, regulates a voluntary union of overseas merchants living and trading in a host city. Its 64 articles bind participants by oath and mutual aid; they do not grant the Hanse territorial sovereignty over Novgorod.

The rules also reveal institutional change. They draw on Lübeck law and were later subjected to, and partly supplanted by, decisions of the Hanseatic Diet. Peterhof therefore belongs in the essay as a merchant compound whose internal discipline was real but nested inside a larger host jurisdiction and an evolving interurban organisation.

The dossier records the commercial treaty tradition from 1191/92 and the suppression of Peterhof in 1494. This profile uses 1295–1494 for the phase attested by the Second Schra and its institutional afterlife; it does not turn either bound into a foundation or dissolution date for the wider Hanse.
regulations: The Second Schra’s 64 articles bound the merchants by oath, required mutual aid, drew on Lübeck law, and were later subjected to regulation by the Hanseatic Diet.
spatial_setting: Peterhof was a merchant settlement inside Novgorod’s political and legal world, occupied by visiting overseas merchants rather than held as Hanseatic territory.
status_phase: Second Schra phase, ending with the suppression of Peterhof in 1494

commodities: Stockfish from northern Norway was the defining export named by UNESCO; this profile encodes no inferred volume or unsupported return-cargo total.
name: Bryggen
notes: Primary witness: Archive of the Hanseatic City of Lübeck, 5.1-1.4 Bergenfahrer, 1039–1047; UNESCO nomination dossier pp. 12–13. Spatial description and stockfish statement cross-checked against the UNESCO Bryggen World Heritage record. place_id is deferred to KAN-306.
profile_summary:
Bryggen was a durable Hanseatic merchant compound on Bergen’s harbour, not a sovereign enclave. UNESCO dates the establishment of the Hanseatic office to about 1350 and describes the surviving urban fabric as offices, dwellings and warehouses. The Crown privileges that sustained the community remained privileges under Norwegian authority.

The court books of 1633–1759 make the institution unusually legible. They record an internal commercial court, communal contributions, fire precautions, office holders and annual price lists. That jurisdiction was practical and substantial, but it was jurisdiction exercised within a host kingdom, which is why the project’s controlled term remains merchant_compound.

Bergen also breaks any simple 1669 ending. The last secretary left in 1761 and the archive moved to Lübeck in 1764. UNESCO’s World Heritage description uses the language of a foreign colony and quasi-extraterritoriality; this project preserves the evidence for autonomy while rejecting colony as a claim of territorial sovereignty.
regulations: Norwegian Crown privileges coexisted with an internal commercial court, communal fees, fire-safety rules, elected office holders and annual price lists recorded in the 1633–1759 court books.
spatial_setting: Bryggen occupied the harbour-front timber rows of Bergen, combining dwellings and offices with warehouses, assembly rooms, kitchens and stone cellars under Norwegian Crown authority.
status_phase: Norwegian-privilege and internal-court phase; the last Kontor secretary departed in 1761

commodities: The ordinance regulates mixed Hanseatic merchandise but supplies no defensible commodity totals; none are inferred from the legal text.
name: Steelyard
notes: Primary witness: Archive of the Hanseatic City of Lübeck, 1.1-3.2 ASA Externa Anglicana, 728; UNESCO nomination dossier p. 12. The rights-cleared Civitates London plate remains the visual section witness and supplies the Steelyard name. place_id is deferred to KAN-306.
profile_summary:
The London Kontor joined a named place to a negotiated legal order. The 1593 Civitates plate calls its house the Gildehalla Teutonica, commonly the Steelyard, and describes the Hanse as a confederated society with four overseas emporia. The view locates the institution inside London’s urban and riverine world rather than outside English sovereignty.

The 1554 by-laws add the institutional detail the plate cannot. Across 30 leaves they regulate elections, internal jurisdiction, finances and community conduct for a body said to represent 66 towns. This was meaningful corporate self-government, but it depended on English privilege and remained exposed to English political decisions.

Suppression in 1598 closes this documented late phase. It does not erase the Steelyard’s earlier history, and the row does not pretend that 1554 was its foundation. The chosen bounds describe the life of the surviving ordinance and the status it helps reconstruct.
regulations: The 1554 by-laws governed elections, internal jurisdiction, finances, social conduct and the training of young merchants; English royal privileges remained the host-law basis of the establishment.
spatial_setting: The community occupied the Gildehalla Teutonica, commonly called the Steelyard, as a merchant house within London and beside its river trade rather than as territory detached from the city.
status_phase: 1554 by-laws phase under English privileges, ending with suppression of the Kontor in 1598

commodities: The 1487 staple covered Hanseatic merchandise moving through Flanders and Brabant; Rhenish wine is specifically attested by the 1502 excise concession.
name: Bruges Kontor
notes: Primary witnesses: City Archives of Bruges, Political charters, 1st series nos. 1016, 1160 and 1434, and 2nd series no. 1617; UNESCO nomination dossier p. 11. The rights-cleared Civitates view remains a separate visual witness. place_id is deferred to KAN-306.
profile_summary:
Bruges makes the Kontor visible through charters rather than through an assumed compound outline on a map. The 1458 documents concern building rights at Oosterlingenplein and a House of Nations. They locate the merchants within a host city whose authorities granted and delimited their privileges.

Later charters add commercial geography: staple rights in 1487 and reduced excise on Rhenish wine in 1502. The sequence is evidence of negotiated access, not of territorial possession. The project therefore uses merchant_compound even though the Bruges institution was more spatially distributed than that shorthand can suggest.

The 1593 Civitates plate says Bruges had once been a most flourishing emporium, placing its commercial primacy in the past without dating a decline. This row’s 1458–1502 bounds are the documentary window of the selected charter group, not the beginning and end of Hanseatic presence in Bruges.
regulations: Charters granted exclusive building rights in 1458, staple rights in 1487 and reduced excise on Rhenish wine in 1502, each a concession from host authorities rather than an assertion of sovereignty.
spatial_setting: The merchants received building rights at Oosterlingenplein and access to a House of Nations, but the documentary geography is a set of negotiated urban sites rather than a walled Hanseatic territory.
status_phase: Chartered Oosterlingenplein, House of Nations and staple-rights phase documented from 1458 to 1502
